extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (Korea); applicants and attorneys preparing/responding to novelty examinations
extracted.subtask_short: determining patent novelty and claim scope
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting claims, defining the claimed invention, assessing prior art scope, and applying novelty rules (including numeric ranges, parameter and product-by-process claims) under the Korean Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identicalness determined by claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision whether an invention is identical is determined by the identicalness of the matters described in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple claims exist, novelty should be determined for each claim individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim language is clear define as recited
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim language is clear, the claimed invention should be defined as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology in claims is interpreted with its general meaning and scope accepted in the technical field, unless the term has a specific meaning explicitly defined in the description. Interpretation should be objective and reasonable, considering technical meaning and a person skilled in the art at filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid limiting claims by description/drawings when claim clear
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is clearly understandable, an examiner should avoid giving it a limited interpretation solely by referencing the description or drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters not described in the claims but only in the description/drawings should be considered not recited in the claims. Conversely, if matters are recited in claims, they should be considered when interpreting the invention. Examiners may consult description/drawings to understand claim subject matter but must not examine claims by applying subject matter not described in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may be broader than embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim subject matter is more comprehensive than embodiments in the description, novelty and inventive step must not be determined by interpreting specific embodiments as the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: generic term 'cream' in claim is not limited to a narrowly disclosed embodiment; 'thin film type probe' claim not limited to a particular tip pattern shown in drawings; rotation direction shown in drawings does not limit a claim that omits rotation direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific definition in description controls if explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant specifically defines a term in the description so it is clearly different from the general meaning, that specific meaning should be used in interpreting the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely describing a specific concept in the description does not automatically constitute a specific definition. Terms should be interpreted consistently across the whole specification; applicants are allowed to define terms, and when explicitly defined the specific definition is applied (Supreme Court precedent cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure or unclear claim terms — examine clarity first
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term in a claim is obscure or unclear, the examiner should determine whether the claimed invention can be grasped by reference to the description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention can be grasped, examiner may notify deficiency in description and novelty collectively. If it remains unclear even with those aids, novelty is not conducted and a rejection for deficiency of description should be issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product defined by function/characteristic construed broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim specifies a product by its work, function, property, or characteristic, it should in principle be construed as every product that has that function/characteristic, unless specifically defined otherwise in the description or limited by common general technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take CGK into account; some uses of 'function' may be understood to exclude technically implausible members (example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' would not be read to apply to magnetic materials difficult to join).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of use (product-by-use) construed as product specially suitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim limits a product by its use, the claimed invention should be interpreted as the product specially suitable for the disclosed use, considering description, drawings, and CGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product with all technical characteristics is not appropriate for the claimed use (or needs conversion), it should not be regarded as the product of the claim. If the limitation of use is not actually suitable in view of the specification/drawings/CGK, the limitation may have no impact on defining the claimed invention and thus not affect novelty (example: agricultural use limitation not preventing anticipation by a catalogue-disclosed fabric if not particularly suited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: process as definition of structure/properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing process recited in a product claim is treated as a means of defining structure or properties of the final product, not as limiting to the process per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/inventive step should be determined by comparing the product having the structure/properties defined by all claim limitations (including process). If the process affects structure/properties, consider process limitations; if the process only affects efficiency/yield and not product properties, novelty is judged by the final product alone. If identical product can be produced by a different process and prior art shows identical product, the claim is not novel. Where it's difficult to determine effect of process, examiner should issue a notice of rejection stating novelty denied and consider applicant arguments; examiner may solicit written arguments or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-type claims: preamble included in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for Jepson-type claims (preamble/body division), the invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements in the preamble are not automatically considered publicly known merely because they are in the preamble; whether preamble elements were publicly known is a factual matter. It is inappropriate to compare only the body with prior art while ignoring the preamble; the technical idea of the invention as a whole (including preamble) is subject matter for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly known invention' for prior art scope
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Publicly known invention' means content known to an unspecified person without secrecy in Korea or abroad before filing; scope of disclosure of a prior art reference is based on what was publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider common general knowledge at filing; if a person skilled in the art can easily arrive at matters described in the reference, those matters are considered publicly known. 'Common general knowledge' includes well-known art and commonly used art (appearing widely in documents, industry, or needless to present examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly practiced invention as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Publicly practiced invention' means an invention practiced under conditions where its contents can be publicly known; actual public knowledge is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be determined based on subject matters embodied in machinery or systems; matters directly derivable from the practice, in light of ordinary skill, can form the basis for finding a publicly practiced invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention in a distributed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described or potentially describable in a publication (i.e., a skilled person can recognize it) is treated as an invention in a distributed publication for prior art purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potentially described means a skilled person can easily recognize the invention from the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain documents (e.g., manuscripts submitted to journals) are not considered publicly known until their contents are released; catalogues generally count as publications unless not published for special reasons; thesis 'publication date' defined as distribution to public or university libraries after final exam unless earlier public announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing date equals publication date, claimed invention does not lose novelty except when filing time is clearly after time of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining novelty by direct comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is determined by comparing the matters defining the claimed invention with matters disclosed in the prior art reference and extracting differences; no difference means not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimed invention is not novel when it is substantially or exactly identical to the prior art disclosure. 'Substantially identical' means no newly produced effect and differences are mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known/common art that do not practically affect the technical idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of inventions with numerical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for claims that include numerical limitations: different outcomes depend on how prior art discloses numbers or ranges relative to the claimed numerical limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four subcases: (1) If prior art has no numerical limitation and claim adds new numbers, invention regarded novel unless the numerical value could be chosen by skilled person or hinted by prior art/CGK (then novelty denied). (2) If claimed numerical range is included in a prior art's range, novelty is not negated automatically — criticality of the range must be shown (technical meaning described in detail; embodiments or supplemental materials proving the range is critical; objective confirmation typically via experimental results covering the range). (3) If claimed range includes a prior art range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If claimed range differs from prior art range, novelty is generally recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty rules for parameter inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameter inventions (applicant creates a new parameter or arithmetic correlation used as an essential claim element) require determining the subject matter from description/drawings/CGK before assessing inventive step and novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claim, but novelty is not established merely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter merely identifies experimentally the nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or is merely a change in expression. If reasonable doubt exists that claimed invention is identical to prior art, examiner may await written arguments or experimental certificates; if doubt unresolved, reject. Examiner must concretely describe grounds for reasonable doubt and may propose ways to overcome rejection. The above rules do not apply when the parameter is standard, commonly used, or easily understandable by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific concept comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim and prior art use generic vs specific concepts, their relationship affects novelty: generic claim vs specific prior art, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ① If claim is generic and prior art is specific (a species), claim is not novel (example: claim to 'metal' anticipated by prior art disclosing Cu). ② If claim is specific and prior art generic, claimed invention generally has novelty, unless the specific embodiment can be directly derived from the generic in view of CGK (then novelty denied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use combinations of multiple prior art for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty determination must not be conducted by comparing a claimed invention with a combination of two or more prior art references; combining references is a matter of inventive step, not novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: when a prior art reference cites a separate publication, that separate publication is regarded as part of the prior art reference and may be relied upon for novelty. Dictionaries and references used to interpret cited reference terms may be treated as cited references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush-type claims: check each alternative against single prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: For Markush-type claims (multiple alternatives), rejection for lack of novelty and inventive step can be notified for each invention alternative using a single prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should assess each claimed alternative (each 'invention') separately against prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine separate embodiments in a single prior art for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art reference contains more than two embodiments, an examiner should not determine novelty by combining two or more of those embodiments; combining embodiments pertains to inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception when one prior art reference is obviously drawn from more than two embodiments considering CGK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant admissions about background art can be treated as published
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant admits in the specification or written arguments that background art is publicly known prior to filing, the examiner can assess novelty assuming that background art was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special circumstances (e.g., mistaken admission about an unpublished prior-filed application or internal company knowledge) can reverse that assumption if applicant proves it; then the ground for rejection based on the assumption may be remedied and examination continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure exceptions (grace period) under Article 30 — substantive rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 30, if a person entitled to obtain a patent files within specified grace periods after certain disclosures (12 months generally, 6 months for earlier filings before March 15, 2012), the invention may be treated as not falling under certain prior art subparagraphs of Article 29.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: encourage applicants to obtain patents after their own disclosure and to encourage early disclosure. KORUS FTA amended Act (Dec 2, 2011) extended grace period to 12 months for applications filed after March 15, 2012. Exceptions: does not apply where the application was laid open or a patent registration published under treaty/law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements to invoke disclosure exception
rubrics_metrics.description: To take advantage of the disclosure exception (Article 30), the filer must submit a written statement of intent and documents proving relevant facts to the Commissioner of KIPO within 30 days of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary fee options allow submission within specified alternative periods (e.g., within amendment period provided in Article 47(1), within 3 months of receipt of certified grant copy or trial decision vacating rejection, subject to limits). Failure to timely submit required statement/proofs can forfeit the exception.
